    Instructor Notes

    These notes help someone teaching this lesson live, in a workshop, class or study group. Each episode is designed to take 45 to 60 minutes of teaching and exercises. You do not need to be a security specialist, but read the episode and its worked solutions before you teach it.

    Running an episode live

    Timing

    • Plan 45 to 60 minutes for each episode, using the minutes shown on the episode page.
    • Each episode has about 20 minutes of teaching and about 35 minutes of challenges, quick check and discussion. Check the minutes on the episode page.
    • If you run short, cut the last challenge before you cut the discussion. The discussion is where learners connect the ideas to their own workplaces.

    Sticky notes

    • Give every learner a pad of sticky notes, or use a shared online board.
    • Use two colours. Green means “I follow this” and pink means “I am stuck”. Learners put the right colour on their laptop or the board at each break.
    • For challenges, learners can write one idea per note, then group the notes on a wall or board.
    • Read the pink notes at each break and answer the most common one first.

    Think-pair-share for discussions

    1. Think (1 minute). Each learner writes their own answer to the discussion question, quietly.
    2. Pair (2 minutes). Learners compare answers with a neighbour and agree on one point to share.
    3. Share (2 minutes). Pairs report back. Write the points where everyone can see them, and ask what is missing.

    Do not rush to give your own view. Ask a pair that disagrees to explain why.

    Using the Riverbend scenario

    • Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the episode that uses it, or allow 3 minutes at the start.
    • Remind learners that the page does not list problems. Finding them is the exercise.
    • If learners add facts that are not on the page, ask them to say they are assumptions.

    Challenges and solutions

    • Learners should attempt each challenge before opening the solution.
    • Solutions are worked answers. Learners’ answers may differ and still be sound. Check the reasoning, not the exact wording.

The editorial was published online in 2019, so confirm which year the course owner wants cited, and update the in-text citation and reference in episode 05 to match.

    11 Privacy law

    • Split. Week-6 video script Parts 1 to 4 (welcome, Privacy Act and APPs, data breaches, 2024 changes, Cyber Security Act). Part 5 (wider world) and Part 6 (the week’s task) are not used here. Week-6 Do 1 is split into two challenges: match ten events to the APP (15 minutes) and “Is it a data breach?” (10 minutes, built on the old Part B and on events 1 and 7). A third step in the second challenge asks why Riverbend is treated “as if” covered.
    • Riverbend and legal framing (decision). Riverbend is council-run, so the APPs and the NDB scheme do not generally bind it; state or territory law does. The episode says so in a short section, states that the exercises “treat Riverbend as if it were covered by the APPs”, and does not name a state. The ten events are recast as separate made-up Riverbend events, with details in the challenge text only. The APP mapping is the same set of principles as the source, because the principles are law content. The worked answer is fresh and uses only the event text, saying “the event does not say” where silent. The OAIC’s own page says the APPs apply to some private sector organisations and most Australian Government agencies, which supports the framing. The ransomware reporting rule is taught with a fictional furniture maker only, and is not applied to Riverbend.
    • Reading. The OAIC and cyber.gov.au pages are free and are in Go deeper. The two Acts are linked on the Federal Register of Legislation. No paid source is used in this episode.
    • Quiz items. 1 bank item (week-6 Q11) and 2 new items adapted from in-video questions. In-video question 2 (café group) was not used.
    • Discussion. None of the week-6 reflection prompts is about breaches or law, so the prompts are reflection prompt 2 (encryption, which links to the technical measures in APP 11) and one new prompt on owning up quickly. The new prompt is there because the no-blame reporting idea in the teaching text needs a prompt of its own.
    • Watch for. Learners saying the APPs bind Riverbend. Learners using APP 11 for every problem or APP 6 for marketing. Learners treating 30 days as a waiting period. Law changes: re-check dates before each run.

    12 Response and future

    • Split. Week-6 video script Part 5 (cybercrime, cyberterrorism, cyber war, the three trends), with the identity-theft response steps from Do 2. Part 6 is not used. Week-6 Do 2 is split into two challenges: Case A, the stolen wallet (15 minutes), and Case B, a message from Riverbend (10 minutes). The week-6 Do 2 worked answer and common-mistakes box give the reasoning structure; both cases are rewritten.
    • Riverbend. Case A is a Riverbend volunteer whose bag is stolen from a public bench, so no organisation is said to be at fault and card G is left out. Case B is a made-up email from Riverbend saying its member database was accessed, without saying how. The worked answer says card G may be added with a condition, and says that for a council-run library the right regulator may be a state or territory body rather than the OAIC, because card G otherwise assumes the Privacy Act. Card G in the challenge says “the regulator that covers it” for the same reason. Card E says “make a report”, not the source’s wording.
    • Reading. Goodman (2015) is paywalled, so it is cited and summarised in one short paragraph from the publisher’s description only, and is not in Go deeper. The excerpt details are still to be confirmed (see Open items), and the text does not depend on them. Publisher and edition are left out of the reference for that reason.
    • Lightly covered topics. Cyber war, cyberterrorism, the Internet of Things, big data, quantum computing and who controls the internet (governments, platforms, your own choices) are covered by a short teaching section and by discussion prompts 1, 3 (partly), 4 and 5. Reflection prompt 2 (encryption) is used in episode 11 instead.
    • Quiz items. 2 bank items (week-6 Q19 and Q23) and 1 new item on a connected device. With episode 11, the week has used 3 of the 3 allowed bank items.
    • Discussion. Week-6 reflection prompts 1, 3, 4 and 5, with a content note on the identity-theft prompt. Learners choose one, so the instructor box says to give pairs different prompts.
    • Watch for. Learners who have been through identity theft: never ask for a personal story. Learners who assume Riverbend or anyone else was at fault. Learners who name the OAIC as Riverbend’s regulator without thinking about the council.

    Digital lives: why we protect data and systems

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes (read aloud in sections, or ask learners to read it first). Exercises 35 minutes: Follow the harm 5, then-and-now challenge 20, quick check 5, discussion 5. The optional interview with a relative is homework, not class time.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners compare technology (“no phones then”) instead of the task. Ask “who did you deal with?” to pull them back.
    • Learners think security only means keeping secrets. Use the hospital example to show that availability and integrity matter as much as confidentiality.
    • Learners assume attackers need technical skill. Leave the answer for episode 2, but plant the question here.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share (see the general notes). The “if it all failed” prompt works well with a short whole-room list of what each pair would lose first.

    Tip. Collect the “new risks” from the then-and-now challenge on a board.


    Social engineering: hacking the human

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 25 minutes, including a pause after the lever table to ask for one real example from the room. Exercises 30 minutes: Spot the phish 10, Name the tactic 10, quick check 5, discussion 5.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners call every scam “phishing”. Use the common-mistakes box to separate the tactics.
    • Learners believe a message is real if the spelling is good or the logo is right. Show that both are cheap to fake.
    • Learners think reporting is an admission of failure. Say clearly that a fast report is a good outcome.
    • In the Name the tactic challenge, several scenarios fit two tactics. Accept a well-reasoned alternative.

    Option 1 of Spot the phish needs internet access. If the room’s network blocks it, use Option 2 as a group exercise and vote on each message.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. Ask pairs which lever they find hardest to resist, and write the answers where everyone can see them.


    Identity, identity management and identity theft

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: Dana case 15, joiner-mover-leaver 10, quick check 5, discussion 5 (2 minutes of quiet writing and 3 minutes of sharing).

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners mix up authentication and authorisation. Use Lucia: the system knew who she was and still said no.
    • Learners think a “password plus PIN” is multi-factor. Ask them to name the kind of proof for each.
    • Learners list effects with no link to the case. Ask “which sentence in the case tells you that?”
    • Learners put the flatmates under “individual”. Ask what connects them to Dana.

    Sensitive topic. Identity theft is personal and some learners will have experienced it. Say before the case that the alternative case is always available and nobody needs to explain why they chose it. Do not ask learners to share their own experiences in the second discussion prompt. Offer IDCARE (see Go deeper) to anyone who needs support.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. On the employer prompt, ask the room to agree what an employer should tell staff about logging, and what limits are fair. There is no single right answer.

    If you are short of time. Drop the joiner-mover-leaver challenge and keep the Dana case.


    The insider threat

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 25 minutes. Exercises 30 minutes: classify 10, choose the control 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Learners can do part A and part B on the same sheet.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners call everything malicious. Keep asking “did the person mean to cause harm?”
    • Learners call Wes negligent because he reused a password. Accept this only if the reason names the reuse and the control fits. The best answer is compromised, because a criminal is the one acting.
    • Learners choose “train staff” for every case. Ask what training would have done for Ruth.
    • Learners blame compromised insiders. Remind them that the person is a victim, and that blame stops people from reporting.
    • Learners think espionage only happens to governments. Mention the small supplier example.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. Do not make the discussion about real organisations or named people. If someone shares a workplace story, ask them to leave out names. The question “which type do organisations most underestimate?” often produces a useful split between negligent and compromised.

    Link to the previous episode. The joiner, mover, leaver cycle (episode 3) is the answer to profile 4. Point this out when learners choose controls.

    If you are short of time. Run part A as a whole-room activity, calling out each profile for a show of hands, and keep part B for pairs.


    Attack techniques and human defences

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: match attacks to defences 15, Mateo 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Learners can do both challenges on the same sheet.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners choose “report it” as the first defence for everything. Ask “what stops the attack happening in the first place?”
    • Learners put a technology fix (a filter, a lock) in the matrix. Remind them that the columns are habits.
    • Learners mix up identity theft and the techniques. Use the bin-raiding example: the bin is how, identity theft is what the criminal achieves.
    • Learners feel it is rude to challenge a visitor. Practise the sentence “Can I help you find someone?” out loud.
    • Learners think espionage is only about governments. Mention the small supplier who is a way into a bigger firm.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The prompt asks about attempts on learners or their families, so do not ask anyone to tell a story. Invite people to share only the defence they would start using first. Keep the IDCARE link visible.

    Tip. If you are short of time, run the matrix as a pair activity and go through the primary column together before the backups.


    Privacy and privacy impact assessments

    Instructor Note

    Timing (58 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 38 minutes: Riverbend threshold assessment 20, two ways to respond 8, quick check 5, discussion 5. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 3 minutes at the start of the first challenge.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think a PIA is only for big projects or big organisations. Ask what a small library would lose if the app leaked children’s allergies.
    • Learners treat “yes, personal information is involved” as the answer. Ask what happens next in the threshold assessment.
    • Learners start fixing the app’s risks. Remind them that the threshold assessment only decides whether to do a PIA.
    • Learners add facts to Riverbend, such as the number of members. Ask them to say “I am assuming”.
    • Learners say “it depends”. Ask them to choose one of the three outcomes and give reasons.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The question about information learners would never want shared can be personal, so ask pairs to share the reason and not the information itself. The answer “both of us” to “who is responsible” is usually correct, so ask what each party’s part is.

    Tip. Collect the pairs’ reasons for the Riverbend decision on a board, then group them by sensitivity, children, new technology and the outside company. Ask which reason is strongest.


    Social media and what attackers can build from it

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: what the profile shows 12, misuse and protection 13, quick check 5, discussion 5.

    Content note. Say at the start that the episode mentions harassment and doxxing in general terms. Tell learners that skipping option (e) is fine. Do not ask anyone to share personal experiences. If a learner is upset, point them to the eSafety Commissioner and, in your own setting, to your usual support.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners list facts and stop. Ask them to point to two posts and say what the pair shows that neither shows alone.
    • Learners write guesses as facts, such as “he lives alone”. Ask where the profile says it, and show them “could”.
    • Learners blame Jonty. Ask what a reasonable person would think about a birthday post.
    • Learners suggest “delete everything”. Ask what Jonty would lose, and whether a smaller audience would do.
    • Learners want to look up a real person to make the task “realistic”. Say no, and explain that profiling a real person is not an acceptable practice exercise.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The prompt asks about personal habits, so ask pairs to share the reason behind a habit and not the details of their accounts. The last question, about why people share despite the risks, tends to produce the best talk: ask what each reason gets the sharer and who pays the cost. For the question about countries that control social media, ask who decides what “protect” means.

    Tip. Run the profile challenge with sticky notes. Give each pair ten post numbers on a board and ask them to draw lines between posts that join. The pattern of lines shows how much more a pair says than a single post.


    People at work: BYOD and working from home

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: score Riverbend’s draft rules 15, weigh the trade and improve the rules 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 3 minutes at the start of the first challenge.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think strict means safe. Ask what a volunteer or staff member would do if the rule made the job much harder.
    • Learners think light means friendly. Ask who pays if a lost phone holds children’s allergy details.
    • Learners score only one column. Hold them to both scores and a reason.
    • Learners add facts to Riverbend or to the drafts, such as how the library would use the app. Ask them to say “the rule does not say” or “I am assuming”.
    • Learners rewrite a rule by deleting it. Ask what the library would lose.
    • Learners treat volunteers like employees. Ask what claim an organisation has on a volunteer’s own phone.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The question about using your own phone for work is personal, so ask pairs to share the condition that would make them comfortable and not their own phone settings. Ask pairs who disagree about where to draw the line to apply the three tests to the same example.

    Tip. Put the eight rules on a board and ask each pair to place a sticky note for each rule on a grid with security gained across and burden up. The rules in the bottom-right corner (high security, low burden) are the good trades. Discuss the ones in the top-left.


    Security awareness that changes behaviour

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: personal ICT check 15, fix the awareness 10, quick check 5, discussion 5.

    Keep the personal check private. Do not ask anyone to read out, show or hand in their checklist, and do not walk around looking at screens. Remind the room that the worked answer is a fictional learner and guidance, not a set of correct personal answers. If you ask for anything at the end, ask only “who has picked a change?” and let people say as much or as little as they like. Remind everyone not to check anyone else’s devices or the venue’s network or router.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think awareness means a policy or a signed form. Ask what a driver or a receptionist did differently on Tuesday.
    • Learners measure attendance or satisfaction. Ask “what would you see if it worked?”
    • Learners choose an enormous change in the personal check. Ask “can you do that tonight?”
    • Learners feel ashamed of their gaps. Say that almost everyone has some.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share (see the general notes), but keep the pair stage general: “what kind of gap did you find?” and not “what is your password habit?” If anyone would rather not talk, let them write only.

    Tip. For the fix-the-awareness challenge, ask pairs to swap plans and check them against the five features, ticking each one.


    Vetting, trust and access

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 25 minutes. Exercises 30 minutes: what did the checks miss 10, limit the reach 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. The Larkspur Marine case is short and is read inside the first challenge.

    Handling the case. The case, Larkspur Marine, is fictional. Keep learners to the text: where it is silent, they say “the scenario does not say” or use “could” or “may”. If learners bring up real cases they know of, keep the focus on controls (“what could have limited the reach of one person?”) rather than on whether the person was right, and treat details offered from memory as unverified.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners say vetting “failed completely” or that it is useless. The point is that a check is a snapshot and one layer.
    • Learners add facts the case does not give. Ask them to use “could” or “may”, or to say the scenario does not say.
    • Learners say compartmentalisation would have prevented the whole event. Ask what it could have reduced.
    • Learners forget the cost to staff, or suggest a control with no owner.
    • Learners think strict checks mean no risk. This links to the second discussion prompt.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share (see the general notes). Ask a pair that disagrees about which change matters most to explain their reasons. The strongest answers say that the three changes work together.

    Tip. Ask pairs to draw a one-line ship on the board and mark which compartment their chosen control would seal.


    Australian privacy law and data breaches

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: match ten events 15, is it a data breach 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 3 minutes at the start of the first challenge.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think small organisations are never covered. Use the health service provider exception.
    • Learners use APP 11 for everything, or APP 6 for marketing. Ask “what stage of the information’s life?” and “is there an opt-out?”.
    • Learners think every breach must be notified, or that 30 days is a waiting period.
    • Learners say the APPs apply to Riverbend because they apply to “privacy”. Ask who runs Riverbend, and what that means for which law applies.
    • Learners add facts to the events. Ask them to say “the event does not say”.

    Running the discussion. The first prompt is personal, so ask pairs to share one habit they could change, not their own settings. For the second, ask what the organisation could do so that reporting feels safe.

    Tip. If you are teaching in a particular state or territory, spend two minutes finding its privacy law for councils and say so aloud. It shows learners that “which law applies” is a real question with a checkable answer. Remind them that this is general information and not legal advice.


    Responding to identity theft, and what comes next

    Instructor Note

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: stolen wallet 15, message from Riverbend 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. The wider-world section is a light overview, so do not spend long on it in the teaching time. The discussion is where it gets airtime. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 2 minutes at the start.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners start with a report to a government service. Ask what stops the money leaving.
    • Learners assume an organisation was at fault in Case A or B. Ask which sentence in the case says so.
    • Learners treat IDCARE as police or a regulator.
    • Learners complain to a regulator before the organisation. Check the order on card G.
    • Learners say Riverbend’s regulator is “the OAIC” without thinking about the council. Ask who runs the library and which law that points to.
    • Learners treat “cyber war” as one agreed idea. Ask them to define “war” first.

    Content note. Identity theft is personal for some learners. Do not ask anyone for their own story. Let them do the exercise as pure ordering and skip the “why” sentences if they prefer. Keep IDCARE visible.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share, with one prompt each for the pairs so that all the topics get covered. Give each pair a different prompt, then ask each pair for one sentence. For the cyber war prompt, ask pairs who disagree to swap definitions of “war”. For the new technology prompt, ask what each trend adds that the learner could change today, such as a router password.

    Tip. Write the eight card letters on cards or sticky notes and let pairs physically order them. Ask them to move a card when Case B is read out.
